110 minutes. Equipment: the display still wired from yesterday and verified in Part 2, the Nucleo, and an AD2 per student -- needed in Part 9, and the debugging instrument if a write does not land earlier. No new components.
The parts as budgeted sum to 107, plus 2 settling, so there is a minute of slack. Re-timed 2026-08-08 after three rounds of cuts: the Arduino material, the I2C_TIMINGR beat, and the Gate 2 repetition census, which took about 7 minutes of duplication out of Parts 3, 5, 8b and 9.
If it runs long, cut in this order: Part 9, which is the stretch; then the Part 4 derivation lever; then Part 1 from 9 to 6. Every part now carries its own trigger on its own section note. NOT cuttable: Part 8b, Part 8c, and Part 8a's layering argument.

slides.title: Where we are
items: Yesterday we used the I2C bus to light up the seven-segment display.
Today we'll look at the backpack chip that drives the display, at the I2C peripheral on the STM32C0, and at the I2C library we handed you yesterday.
We'll start with the display and its controller, then the I2C1 peripheral and the two pins through which it reaches the wires, then the library.
By the end of today your own display will show ES.28, written out of a ten-byte buffer by a device driver you wrote. You'll use that driver in Lab 5.
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min with announcements. 110 minutes today, against 50 yesterday — say that, because the pace is genuinely different.

Recap
items: 34 LEDs reached through 14 backpack pins, because a grid saves wires and a sweep buys back the one digit at a time it costs you. The backpack runs that sweep so your program does not have to.
A device's commands come out of its datasheet's command table, one byte each, and the header's names are from that table's structure.
The display uses two bytes per digit position, five positions; the odd bytes are needed because the pointer advances on every byte, and all ten in one transaction.
PB8 and PB9 are AF6, and open-drain is what lets SDA change hands every ninth bit.
One assignment to I2C_CR2 describes an entire transaction.
A device driver reaches the hardware only through the interface driver, never a machine register.
The scope can answer 'did my bytes arrive?', and the datasheet helps you tell 'were they the right bytes?'
